Bekah Brunstetter’s book, adapted from Sparks’ novel, leans on familiar tropes: soulmates pulled apart by circumstance, disapproving parents and the inevitable reunion. But there’s power in those timeless beats, especially when they’re brought to life by a cast of this caliber.
All of it presents a beautiful picture of mortality, but also the universality of love.
Yet the core of the story, a devoted spouse's attempt to connect with the wife whose mind has almost entirely slipped away, never fails.

The music's strength is not in big memorable show tunes but rather in its ability to register feelings of love and loss.
Ingrid Michaelson's lush music is by far the strongest element of 'The Notebook: The Musical,' even if uniform motifs occasionally blend one song with the next.
The touring production of "The Notebook," onstage at the Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts, really wants you to cry.

Under the direction of Michael Greif and Schele Williams, a couple of well-done moments provide brief relief. In the song “Forever,” when the Middles reunite, a lusty Middle Allie, finding out Noah built the table where she’s seated, buries her face in its woodsy smell and suggestively strokes its leg.

The story has its shimmering moments — “where do we go, when we go?” the Noahs and Allies sing near the end — but ultimately the couple’s only adversary is time, which is, unfortunately, not a particularly compelling dramatic foil here.

Ultimately, the musical feels like it needed another round of development to become truly compelling. But when the source material itself is so middle-of-the-road (albeit enormously popular), there’s only so much that can be added.
The acting talent of Beau Gravitte as Older Noah was particularly poignant, and Yassmin Alers as Older Allie was convincing as a woman struggling with memory loss.
